question: Can the outputs of heterogeneous trained neural networks on all masks of a chosen input be represented faithfully by a small set of AND-OR interactions, and do simple properties of the average response to masking explain why such interactions are sparse and transferable?

key_findings.claim: A sparse AND-OR model can reconstruct the probed network output over the complete mask lattice of a small chosen variable set.
key_findings.evidence: The method fits additive AND and OR effects under a uniform output-error tolerance over every one of the 2^n masked states. Retaining only the 100 largest-magnitude interactions plus a bias yields a reported coefficient of determination of 0.997±0.002 across the evaluated CNN, LLM, and PointNet cases.

key_findings.claim: The fitted interaction representation is empirically sparse across architectures, modalities, and model sizes within the chosen 9-10-variable problems.
key_findings.evidence: Across VGG and ResNet image classifiers, Qwen2.5, DeepSeek-R1-distilled and Phi-4 language models, and PointNet, the mean number of salient effects ranges from 10.2 to 79.1 despite up to 2^(n+1) candidate AND and OR effects. The reported sparsity does not change monotonically with LLM size.

anchors.section: Emergence of sparse interactions across diverse ANNs and tasks

key_findings.claim: Monotonic and smooth average response to the number of retained variables is sufficient for a small aggregate sparsity bound when positive and negative effects do not almost perfectly cancel.
key_findings.evidence: The theory reduces each input to its order-averaged sequence v̄(k), assumes that it increases with k and has bounded second finite difference, and bounds salient interactions through an optimized quantity M and cancellation coefficient η. Across 10,000 sampled admissible sequences, the 95th percentile of M is at most 7.8, 23.3, and 108.5 for n=10, 20, and 40. Empirically η exceeds 0.1 for 96.6% of LLM samples and 86.9% of CNN samples, with means 0.376 and 0.247.

anchors.section: Mathematical criteria for the emergence of sparse interactions

key_findings.claim: Low-order interaction patterns overlap across separately trained LLM families on the same prompt and target token.
key_findings.evidence: For Qwen2.5-7B versus DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B and Phi-4 versus DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, effects are decomposed into shared and model-specific components. First- and second-order terms have the strongest reported sharedness; the authors avoid strong conclusions for orders 8-10 because so few such effects remain.

key_findings.claim: A small category-level dictionary recovers many salient interactions across samples when semantic parts are manually aligned.
key_findings.evidence: A dictionary of the 100 most frequent effects covers on average 83.0% of salient interactions for 50 CelebA eyeglasses images and 68.7% for 100 ShapeNet motorbikes. Each example is represented by the same nine annotated face or motorbike parts.

anchors.section: Transferability of interactions across different samples

key_findings.claim: The proposed interaction order correlates with a constructed notion of generalization and changes systematically over training.
key_findings.evidence: An interaction is called generalizable when it is salient with the same sign in a target VGG-16 trained on one Tiny-ImageNet half and a baseline VGG-16 trained on the held-out half. More than 70% of first-order effect is generalizable versus 32.75% at sixth order; 42.7% of positive effect versus 31.6% of negative effect is generalizable. At eight epochs low orders dominate, while medium and high orders later rise during the reported overfitting phase.

anchors.section: Using interactions to explain the performance of an ANN

method.core_idea: Project a network's scalar behavior on every mask of a small input-variable set into an additive symbolic basis whose atoms fire under AND or OR presence rules, then relate the number and transfer of large coefficients to the response curve averaged by mask order.
method.mechanism: Choose 9-13 image regions, phrases, or semantic 3D parts; replace absent variables with an embedding, feature, or geometric baseline; and query a target logit or next-token log-odds on all 2^n masks. Solve an L1-style constrained program for sparse AND and OR effects with tolerance 0.02 times the expected full-versus-empty output span. Analyze sparsity by effect magnitude, compare sign-consistent effects across models and samples, and track order-resolved effects through VGG training. For theory, collapse the mask lattice to v̄(k), the mean output when k variables remain, and impose monotonicity and bounded second difference.
assumptions: The selected patches, phrases, or parts form the relevant variable universe for the explanation.
The chosen mask baseline represents absence without introducing an unintended feature or distribution shift.
A scalar target logit or next-token log-odds adequately represents the network decision being explained.
Sparse AND and OR effects are a meaningful symbolic basis rather than merely one convenient Möbius-style decomposition of a finite function table.
Salience magnitude and sign are comparable across samples or separately trained models once variables are semantically aligned.
The order-averaged response v̄(k) is monotone and sufficiently smooth for most relevant trained-model inputs, and cancellation coefficient η is not too small.
Overlap with a model trained on held-out examples is a useful proxy for an interaction's generalization.

techniques.role: Queries every subset of a small selected variable set so reconstruction is evaluated over the complete finite domain.
Fits additive logical trigger effects under an L1-style objective and a uniform output-error constraint.
Collapses exponentially many masks into the mean output v̄(k) for each number of retained variables.
Bounds changes in marginal confidence by constraining the second finite difference of v̄(k).
Measures how much positive and negative interaction mass cancels, converting an aggregate bound into a salient-effect count.
Labels an interaction shared when the same variable subset is salient with the same sign in two models.
Ranks frequent effects across examples with manually corresponding components and measures per-sample coverage.
Uses interactions of a same-architecture model trained on held-out examples as an operational reference for generalizability.
Tracks normalized positive and negative effect mass by interaction order over 256 training epochs.

evaluations.setting: VGG-16 and ResNet-18/34/50 on 1,000 ImageNet validation images, ten high-activation feature blocks
evaluations.metric: Number of salient effects and R² of top-100 logical reconstruction
evaluations.result: Part of the reported 10.2-79.1 salient-count range and pooled R² 0.997±0.002
evaluations.baseline: Full ANN outputs on all 1,024 masks

evaluations.setting: Qwen2.5 0.5B-14B, DeepSeek-R1-distilled 1.5B-14B, and Phi-4 on 100 hand-constructed topical sentences with ten phrases
evaluations.metric: Interaction sparsity and cross-model order-wise shared effect
evaluations.result: Sparse effects across sizes; first and second orders have the strongest shared component
evaluations.baseline: All candidate AND-OR subsets and model-specific effects

evaluations.setting: PointNet on 100 ShapeNet motorbikes with nine annotated semantic parts
evaluations.metric: Salient interaction count and category-dictionary coverage
evaluations.result: A 100-effect dictionary covers 68.7% of each sample's salient interactions on average

evaluations.setting: ResNet-50 on 50 CelebA eyeglasses images with nine annotated face components
evaluations.result: A 100-effect dictionary covers 83.0% of salient interactions on average

evaluations.setting: 10,000 sampled monotone, C-smooth v̄(k) sequences for each n, C, and epsilon setting
evaluations.result: At most 7.8 for n=10, 23.3 for n=20, and 108.5 for n=40 over the reported settings
evaluations.baseline: Up to 2^(n+1) candidate AND and OR effects

evaluations.setting: Two VGG-16 models trained on disjoint Tiny-ImageNet halves and one 256-epoch VGG training trajectory
evaluations.metric: Shared-effect ratio by order and normalized effect dynamics
evaluations.result: Generalizable share declines from above 70% at first order to 32.75% at sixth order; medium/high-order mass rises in the late overfitting phase

limitations: Author-stated: AND-OR interactions are only one projection of a network's oracle inference patterns and are not fully equivalent to the function the ANN truly models.
Author-stated: the current theory is formulated for scalar outputs; multiclass and multidimensional behavior must be reduced to one selected logit or log-odds value.
Reviewer-identified: exact enumeration scales as 2^n, restricting the empirical explanation to 9-13 selected variables even when the original input has thousands of tokens, pixels, or points.

Reviewer-identified: variables and absence baselines are manually selected or chosen by high activation; changing either can change the entire interaction basis, sparsity, monotonicity, and apparent transfer.

Reviewer-identified: the fitting objective explicitly penalizes L1 interaction mass, so observed sparsity is partly imposed by the estimator; comparison with alternative sparse bases and non-sparse exact decompositions is absent.
Reviewer-identified: top-100 fidelity is evaluated on the same finite mask lattice used for extraction, not on natural perturbations, new prompts, or causal edits outside that constructed domain.

Reviewer-identified: the sparsity bound uses only order-averaged outputs and a cancellation coefficient; it establishes existence under aggregate conditions, not uniqueness, semantic meaning, or recovery of the network's actual internal mechanism.

Reviewer-identified: cross-sample transfer uses manually homologous semantic parts, while cross-model transfer uses the same prompt, chosen target token, salience rule, and sign; this alignment makes overlap easier and does not localize shared circuits.

Reviewer-identified: a model trained directly on the held-out split is an unusual oracle for 'generalizability'; shared effects may reflect architecture and mask artifacts rather than the mechanism that caused ordinary test generalization.
Reviewer-identified: the proposed communicative-learning paradigm is speculative; no experiment edits an interaction and shows predictable, localized behavioral change.
failure_modes: An off-manifold mask baseline can create large artificial interactions that describe the corruption process rather than natural inference.
A different grouping of tokens or image patches can split one effect or merge several effects, destroying claimed sparsity and transfer without changing the underlying network.
Strong positive-negative cancellation makes η small and the sparsity bound vacuous even when v̄(k) remains monotone and smooth.
A model can have a smooth order-averaged response while individual masks vary sharply, because averaging hides heterogeneous or adversarial states.
The L1 program can select one of many equivalent AND-OR decompositions, so coefficient identity may be unstable under small output noise or tolerance changes.
Shared low-order effects can arise from common architecture, data preprocessing, or label priors without representing the same internal computation.
High-order but essential rare-case logic can appear non-generalizable under average magnitude even though it controls safety-critical inputs.
For LLMs, replacing phrase embeddings with a fixed baseline can alter position, syntax, and attention globally, confounding a phrase's absence with an unnatural sequence state.
reusable_insights: Separate representation fidelity from semantic validity: reproducing a function table is necessary but does not by itself identify a meaningful mechanism.
Report how explanation complexity changes with the variable partition and absence baseline, not only with model architecture or size.
Use the response curve indexed by number of retained variables as a compact diagnostic of monotonicity, curvature, and mask-distribution artifacts.
Measure both shared effect identity and the fraction of output magnitude it explains; raw set overlap can overvalue tiny coefficients.
Align semantic variables explicitly before testing cross-sample transfer, while acknowledging that the alignment supplies part of the result.
Trace interaction order over training to form falsifiable predictions about when memorization or overfitting begins.
Validate symbolic edits causally and on natural inputs before using extracted effects as a human-facing control interface.
open_questions: Can sparse interaction recovery scale beyond 40 variables without assuming the very sparsity it is meant to discover?
Which sparsity and transfer conclusions survive across multiple absence baselines, token segmentations, and image partitions?
Can an interaction be causally localized to parameters or circuits and edited without widespread collateral effects?
Does interaction-dictionary coverage predict ordinary held-out performance better than simpler attribution, margin, or representation-similarity baselines?
Can the monotonicity and smoothness criteria be measured with confidence bounds from sampled masks rather than exhaustive enumeration?
Are high-order late-training effects causes of overfitting, consequences of confidence growth, or artifacts of the normalized log-odds and masking procedure?
Can a basis-selection criterion distinguish genuinely symbolic primitives from sparse approximations available in many interchangeable dictionaries?
How do multi-output, autoregressive sequence-level, and stochastic model behaviors alter the universal-matching and sparsity claims?

competitive_landscape.title: Where We Have Arrived in Proving the Emergence of Sparse Symbolic Concepts in AI Models
competitive_landscape.difference: This closest same-group predecessor already proves sparse interaction emergence and faithful reconstruction on exponentially many masks under three sufficient conditions involving high-order derivatives, confidence monotonicity under occlusion, and limited degradation. The present paper replaces that condition set with monotonicity and second-difference smoothness of the order-averaged response, adds OR terms and substantially broader cross-modal evidence, but the central emergence thesis is not new.

competitive_landscape.title: Does a Neural Network Really Encode Symbolic Concepts?
competitive_landscape.difference: Li and Zhang already test whether interaction concepts are sparse, transferable, discriminative, and partly human-aligned. The present work adds a two-criterion aggregate sparsity argument, more recent LLM families, PointNet, AND-OR reconstruction, and training/generalization analyses, while inheriting the same mask-based concept semantics.

competitive_landscape.title: Defining and Extracting generalizable interaction primitives from DNNs
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen et al. explicitly optimize interactions shared by multiple DNNs to isolate generalizable primitives. The present paper uses simpler sign-consistent overlap and a test-trained reference model, integrating cross-model convergence into a broader emergence narrative rather than introducing the first transferable-interaction method.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards the Dynamics of a DNN Learning Symbolic Interactions
competitive_landscape.difference: Ren et al. develop a theory and experiments for two-phase learning of low- versus high-order interactions and connect the transition to overfitting. The present paper reuses that interaction-order lens and supplies an additional VGG trace and held-out overlap analysis; its principal new theory concerns static sparsity, not training dynamics.

competitive_landscape.title: Emergent Symbolic Mechanisms Support Abstract Reasoning in Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang et al. identify and intervene on a three-stage circuit of abstraction, symbolic induction, and retrieval heads in Llama3-70B. This paper is architecture-agnostic and exhaustively decomposes masked input-output behavior, but it does not localize neurons or circuits; the two works use materially different meanings of 'symbolic mechanism.'

novelty_assessment: Author claim: two common architecture-agnostic mathematical criteria make sparse symbolic interactions emerge as a natural law across neural networks, and their fidelity, model-to-model convergence, sample transfer, and generalization explain broad ANN behavior. Reviewer inference: the strongest incremental contribution is the particular monotonicity-plus-finite-difference formulation of an aggregate sparsity bound, combined with a single broad empirical package spanning modern LLMs, CNNs, and point clouds. The core AND/OR interaction representation, universal masked-state matching, sparsity thesis, transferable effects, and two-phase training interpretation have substantial prior coverage by the same research program. The evidence supports a useful sparse functional projection on small hand-constructed mask lattices; it does not establish a unique internal symbolic language or an architecture-independent natural law.
reviewer_notes: All substantive text through page 18 was checked, including variable construction, masking baselines, optimization tolerance, sampled-sequence theory, transfer protocol, test-trained reference model, and 256-epoch dynamics. A few displayed equations were corrupted in PDF text extraction, so the review reports only relationships that were legible in both the main explanation and methods. Competitive claims were checked against primary arXiv or OpenReview records current through 2026-08-23.
